newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia farming suffers $75 mln weather damage. [CORRECTED 17:08 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia farming suffers $75 mln weather damage. [CORRECTED 17:08 GMT]

text.p: Bad weather which hit Yugoslavia in June and July has seriously damaged crops on some 200,000 hectares causing a 450 million dinar ($75.8 million) loss, a senior government official said on Friday.

"Heavy rains and hailstorms from June 17 to 20 and in the first decade (10 days) of July have caused enormous damage to crops in Vojvodina and the central part of Serbia," Jan Kisgeci of the federal Agriculture Ministry said.
"The extent of the damage is still being evaluated but according to the first estimates the loss is some 450 million dinars," he told a news conference.
In the country's bread-basket of Vojvodina alone some 139,000 hectares were hit by bad weather, or 8.5 percent of the total arable land.
Wheat was damaged on some 32,000 ha, maize on 61,000 ha and sunflowers on some 13 ha.
Damage ranged from 10 to 100 percent, but mostly from 30 to 70 percent of the crops in the areas hit.
"In Vojvodina alone, the loss is 337 million dinars or 2,440 (corrects from 4,440) dinars per hectare," Kisgeci said.
Many of the areas must be re-sown, some using high-quality hybrids and seeds provided by the government.

Ljiljana Vasic, head of the Association of Agricultural Cooperatives of Vojvodina, told Reuters many farmers had lost their entire crop and needed help to re-start production due to their already difficult financial situation.
"The state must help them by securing some additional funds and by extending their liabilities by at least another two years."
The federal government, according to Kisgeci, had proposed a whole range of emergency measures to ease the economic position of cooperatives and farms hit by the bad weather.
It had proposed that the Federal Commodity Reserve Agency freeze repayment of farm credits it approved for a period of one year and extend repayment over the next three.

The central and commercial banks were asked to postpone repayments of posted credits to agricultural firms which suffered losses until the year-end and convert them to 10-year loans for constant working capital.

"We have proposed that the 1997 interest be halved for those firms whose losses are lower than 25 percent of their production, and written off completely for those where losses exceed 25 percent," Kisgeci said.
The government suggested that both central and commercial banks grant favourable loans to firms which suffered losses to help them restart production.
Some five million dinars would also be secured from the federal budget to finance construction of anti-hail defences in those areas where they did not exist, Kisgeci said.
"There is a serious danger that agricultural producers, with already exhausted funds, do not invest in new production this fall due to a lack of resources," he added.
